1 Kings 1: David is old, and Adonijah claims the throne at En-rogel while Solomon is anointed at Gihon, Jerusalem's spring. Solomon's reign is usually dated about 970–931 BC.
1 Kings 2: David dies after reigning forty years (1 Kings 2:11), and Solomon secures the throne in Jerusalem.
1 Kings 3: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter and sacrifices at Gibeon, "the great high place" (1 Kings 3:4), since the temple is not yet built.
1 Kings 4: Solomon's officials and twelve district governors supply the court. His rule reaches "from the river unto the land of the Philistines, and unto the border of Egypt" (1 Kings 4:21).
1 Kings 5: Hiram king of Tyre, a Phoenician port city, supplies cedar and fir from Lebanon in exchange for wheat and oil.
1 Kings 6: Building begins in the 480th year after the exodus, in Solomon's fourth year, in the month Zif (1 Kings 6:1), and takes seven years (1 Kings 6:38).
1 Kings 7: Solomon spends thirteen years building his palace (1 Kings 7:1). Hiram of Tyre, a bronze worker, casts the temple's pillars and vessels in the Jordan plain.
1 Kings 8: The ark is brought into the temple at the feast in the seventh month, Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2), in autumn.
1 Kings 9: After twenty years of building (1 Kings 9:10), Solomon fortifies Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer and builds a fleet at Eziongeber on the Red Sea.
1 Kings 10: The queen of Sheba, a kingdom usually placed in southern Arabia, visits Jerusalem. Solomon trades in gold, horses, and chariots.
1 Kings 11: Late in Solomon's reign, Hadad of Edom, Rezon of Damascus, and Jeroboam rise against him. Solomon dies after forty years (1 Kings 11:42).
1 Kings 12: At Shechem the northern tribes reject Rehoboam and make Jeroboam king, about 930 BC. Jeroboam sets up golden calves at Bethel and Dan.
1 Kings 13: A man of God from Judah prophesies against Jeroboam's altar at Bethel, naming a future king, Josiah (1 Kings 13:2).
1 Kings 14: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt attacks Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:25). Pharaoh Shoshenq I's inscription at Karnak lists towns he took in this region about 925 BC.
1 Kings 15: Abijam and Asa reign in Judah, and Nadab and Baasha in Israel. Asa pays Benhadad of Damascus to attack Israel.
1 Kings 16: Omri becomes king of Israel and builds Samaria as his capital (1 Kings 16:24). The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) names Omri as king of Israel. Ahab begins his reign.
1 Kings 17: Elijah announces a drought to Ahab. He hides by the brook Cherith, east of the Jordan, then stays at Zarephath, a Phoenician town near Sidon.
1 Kings 18: In the third year of the drought, Elijah faces the prophets of Baal on mount Carmel, above the coast near modern Haifa.
1 Kings 19: Elijah flees from Jezebel to Beersheba and travels forty days to Horeb, the mount of God.
1 Kings 20: Benhadad of Syria besieges Samaria, then is defeated at Aphek.
1 Kings 21: Ahab seizes Naboth's vineyard beside his palace in Jezreel.
1 Kings 22: Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah fight Syria at Ramothgilead, where Ahab dies, about 853 BC. Assyrian records list Ahab at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC.
2 Kings 1: Ahab's son Ahaziah falls in Samaria and sends to Baalzebub, god of the Philistine city Ekron.
2 Kings 2: Elijah is taken up near the Jordan, across from Jericho, and Elisha returns by way of Jericho and Bethel.
2 Kings 3: During the divided kingdom, Israel, Judah, and Edom campaign against Moab in the wilderness of Edom (2 Kings 3:4–9).
2 Kings 4: During Elisha’s ministry in Israel, he travels among places including Shunem, Gilgal, and Jericho (2 Kings 4:8–44).
2 Kings 5: Naaman, commander of the army of Syria, comes from Damascus to Elisha in Samaria and washes in the Jordan.
2 Kings 6: Syria raids Israel. Elisha is at Dothan, and Benhadad besieges Samaria, causing great famine.
2 Kings 7: The Syrian siege of Samaria ends when the army flees in the night.
2 Kings 8: Hazael murders Benhadad and takes the throne of Damascus. An Assyrian inscription calls Hazael ‘son of a nobody,’ a usurper.
2 Kings 9: Jehu is anointed at Ramothgilead and kills Joram of Israel and Ahaziah of Judah, about 841 BC. Jezebel dies at Jezreel.
2 Kings 10: After Jehu becomes king, he destroys Ahab’s house in Jezreel and Samaria and confronts Baal worship in Samaria (2 Kings 10:1–28).
2 Kings 11: Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, seizes Judah's throne for six years until seven-year-old Joash is crowned in the temple.
2 Kings 12: Joash repairs the temple and pays tribute to Hazael of Syria to keep him from Jerusalem.
2 Kings 13: Israel is weakened by Hazael. Elisha dies, and Joash of Israel recovers cities from Syria.
2 Kings 14: Amaziah of Judah defeats Edom in the valley of salt, then is defeated by Jehoash of Israel. Jeroboam II restores Israel's borders in the early 8th century BC.
2 Kings 15: Azariah (Uzziah) reigns in Judah fifty-two years. Israel has six kings in quick succession, and Tiglathpileser of Assyria takes Galilee and Gilead (2 Kings 15:29), about 733 BC.
2 Kings 16: Ahaz of Judah pays Tiglathpileser to rescue him from Syria and Israel. Assyria takes Damascus in 732 BC.
2 Kings 17: Shalmaneser V besieges Samaria for three years, and it falls in Hoshea's ninth year (2 Kings 17:5–6), 722 BC. Israelites are deported and foreigners settled in Samaria.
2 Kings 18: Hezekiah reigns in Judah. In his fourteenth year, 701 BC, Sennacherib of Assyria takes Judah's walled cities, including Lachish. Sennacherib's own annals record shutting Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage.
2 Kings 19: Sennacherib's army is struck down outside Jerusalem, and he returns to Nineveh. He was killed by his sons in 681 BC.
2 Kings 20: Hezekiah is healed and lives fifteen more years. Merodachbaladan of Babylon sends envoys; he was a Chaldean leader who fought Assyria for years.
2 Kings 21: Manasseh reigns fifty-five years in Jerusalem (2 Kings 21:1), about 697–642 BC, as a vassal of Assyria. Amon follows briefly.
2 Kings 22: In Josiah's eighteenth year, 622 BC, the book of the law is found during temple repairs.
2 Kings 23: Josiah destroys the altar at Bethel and keeps Passover. He dies at Megiddo in 609 BC facing Pharaoh Necho, who was marching north to help Assyria.
2 Kings 24: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon takes Jerusalem and carries Jehoiachin to Babylon in 597 BC. The Babylonian Chronicle records this capture.
2 Kings 25: Jerusalem falls in Zedekiah's eleventh year, in the fifth month (2 Kings 25:2, 8), 586 BC. The book ends with Jehoiachin released from prison in Babylon about 562 BC.
